question: Does a network volume carry a CUDA build between pods, and what does a multi-architecture (fat) binary cost?
answer: Yes. The same key hit on a second, separate pod and the whole run took 3 min 3 s with no compilation, against a 12 min 31 s fat build on the first. The fat binary costs 2.07x the size and nothing measurable at runtime.

volume.name: mizu-build-cache
volume.note: df on the mount reports the whole MooseFS pool (700 T), not the 10 GB quota, so du on the cache directory is the only honest way to watch it.

fat_build.separator_note: the fork's CMake does string(REPLACE "," ";" ...), so the value is comma-separated

proof_equivalence.reading: +1.4% of wall, inside the 0.8-0.9% within-side spread measured for this host class, so the cached fat binary proves the same statement at the same speed. The proof hashes differ because FRI draws randomness.

driver_fixes_this_exposed: ROOT and RESULTS defaulted into /workspace, i.e. onto the mounted volume, so an unpacked tree and a results directory survived the pod and would block the next run; both now default to container disk and only the cache lives on the volume
push-and-launch.sh did not forward RESULTS, and the watchdog hardcoded its log directory; both parameterised
collect-results.sh hardcoded /workspace/results in five places and staged its archives on the volume; it now takes POD_RESULTS and stages on container disk
limits: CUDA_ARCHS is part of the cache key, so a run that lets the driver auto-detect from the card computes 86 and misses a 86,89,120 cache. A superset ought to count as a hit; it does not yet.
One hit, one miss. No measurement of what happens when the key moves for a source edit.
Run 1's leftovers from the old defaults (an unpacked tree, a results directory, an evidence tarball, the two scp'd scripts) are still on the volume, about 100 MB; harmless but not cleaned.
No off-pod verification in either run: proof bytes stayed on the pod by request.

cost.volume_standing_cost: 10 GB from creation until deletion; rate not exposed by the tools
